Cape Canaveral, 2011-11-26. Mars Science Laboratory carries Curiosity, the largest, most capable rover at the time (900 kg, plutonium-powered RTG, mission lifetime targets 1 Mars year (687 days) — actually 12+ years and counting). Launched on the second-largest Atlas V configuration available.
Centaur upper stage burn at T+45 minutes accelerates MSL onto a Hohmann-like transfer to Mars. Cruise stage handles solar panels + attitude control during the ~8.5-month cruise.

Cleanup burn on 2012-01-11, about 46 days after launch, removing the small dispersion from the launch + TMI. Standard Mars-cruise practice: schedule TCMs at lengthening intervals as the trajectory firms up.
Mid-cruise refinement burn. By this point Curiosity is past Earth's gravity well and on a stable heliocentric trajectory.
Approach-phase pre-burn. Begins tightening the targeting for the Gale Crater EDL site.
TCM-4 — fourth correction (two more chances remained before landing)
Last large trajectory tweak before Mars entry. EDL requires <1 km targeting accuracy at the atmospheric interface; TCM-4 delivers it.
2012-08-06 UTC (the evening of 5 August in California). 10 minutes before atmospheric entry, the cruise stage separates and the backshell + descent stage + rover hits Mars's atmosphere at 5.85 km/s.
Mars EDL — sky-crane landing in Gale Crater

"Seven minutes of terror": the parachute deploys, then the descent stage fires retro-rockets and lowers Curiosity on a 7.5-m sky-crane tether — a one-shot technique no Mars mission had used before. Landed 2012-08-06 05:17 UTC (the signal reached Earth at 22:32 PDT on 5 August) at 4.5895°S, 137.4417°E, a few hundred metres from target inside Gale Crater. The first Hazcam images came within minutes; the first panorama followed on 7 August. Still operational 12+ years on, climbing Mount Sharp's stratigraphic column.
First nuclear-powered Mars rover; first sky-crane landing

Curiosity is a nuclear-powered laboratory the size of a small car, and getting it down was the hard part. Too heavy for airbags, it was lowered onto Mars in 2012 by a rocket-powered sky crane in a sequence so risky its planners called it seven minutes of terror — and it worked on the first try. Since then it has drilled its way across Gale Crater and answered the question it was sent to ask: the crater once held a lake, with the chemistry a living thing could have used. Mars had been habitable. Curiosity is still driving, climbing a mountain of layered rock that reads like the planet’s own history book.

The flagship mission that defined modern Mars exploration. Curiosity is car-sized, plutonium-powered, and has driven 36+ km across Gale Crater since landing in 2012. Its instruments confirmed Mars once had habitable conditions — flowing water, complex organics, the chemistry life would need. The 'seven minutes of terror' EDL sequence, ending with a sky-crane lowering the rover on cables, is now NASA's standard for delivering large payloads to Mars surface.
Atlas V 541 lifts off from Cape Canaveral SLC-41.
Trans-Mars injection sends MSL onto a heliocentric Mars-bound trajectory.
Third trajectory correction; refines the Gale Crater target.
Atmospheric entry, supersonic parachute, sky-crane retro-rockets, rover lowered on cables.
Curiosity arrives at Aeolis Palus, Gale Crater, 2012-08-06 05:17:57 UTC.
Hazcam returns first low-resolution image of the surface.
